chapter_text:
CHAPTER 17 - MAGNETIC EFFECT OF ELECTRIC CURRENT

Introduction

Electricity and magnetism were once thought to be entirely separate phenomena. In 1820 the Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted made a chance discovery that linked them forever: an electric current flowing through a wire deflects a nearby magnetic compass needle. This single observation showed that a current-carrying conductor behaves like a magnet, and it launched the whole subject of electromagnetism. In this chapter we study the magnetic field produced by electric currents, the force a magnetic field exerts on a current, the electric motor that turns electrical energy into motion, electromagnetic induction (the reverse process discovered by Faraday), the electric generator, and finally the wiring and safety devices of the domestic electric circuit.

17.1 MAGNETS AND THE MAGNETIC FIELD

A magnet is a body that attracts magnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt. Every magnet has two poles - a north (N) pole and a south (S) pole. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest pointing roughly north-south, which is how the magnetic compass works. Magnetic poles always occur in pairs; if a magnet is cut in two, each piece becomes a complete magnet with its own N and S pole.

The region around a magnet (or a current) in which its magnetic influence can be detected is called its MAGNETIC FIELD. The magnetic field is a vector quantity - it has both magnitude and direction. Its direction at any point is taken as the direction in which the north pole of a tiny test compass would point. The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is the tesla (T).

17.2 MAGNETIC FIELD LINES

A convenient way to picture a magnetic field is to draw MAGNETIC FIELD LINES (lines of force). The pattern of iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet traces out these lines. Their properties are:
 - Field lines emerge from the N pole and enter the S pole outside the magnet; inside the magnet they run from S to N, so each line forms a closed loop.
 - The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the field there.
 - The lines are crowded together where the field is strong (near the poles) and spread out where it is weak.
 - Two field lines never cross one another - if they did, the field would have two directions at one point, which is impossible.

17.3 OERSTED'S EXPERIMENT - CURRENT PRODUCES MAGNETISM

Oersted placed a compass needle below a straight wire lying along the north-south direction. When no current flowed, the needle stayed parallel to the wire. The moment a current was switched on, the needle was deflected sideways; reversing the current reversed the deflection. This proved that an electric current sets up a magnetic field around itself. The magnetic effect of current is the foundation of electromagnets, motors and generators.

17.4 MAGNETIC FIELD DUE TO A STRAIGHT CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR

Around a long straight wire the magnetic field lines are CONCENTRIC CIRCLES centred on the wire and lying in planes perpendicular to it. The field is stronger close to the wire (circles crowded) and weaker farther away (circles spread out); it also increases if the current increases. The direction of the field is given by:
 - RIGHT-HAND THUMB RULE: grasp the wire with the right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of the conventional current; the curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines.
 - MAXWELL'S CORKSCREW RULE: if a right-handed corkscrew is turned so that its tip advances in the direction of the current, the direction in which the handle rotates gives the direction of the field.

17.5 MAGNETIC FIELD DUE TO A CIRCULAR LOOP

If the straight wire is bent into a circular loop, every small part of the loop produces circular field lines around it. At the centre of the loop these contributions add up so that the field there is nearly straight and perpendicular to the plane of the loop. One face of the loop behaves like a north pole and the other like a south pole. The field at the centre is increased by increasing the current, by increasing the number of turns (each turn adds its field), and by decreasing the radius of the loop.

17.6 SOLENOID AND ELECTROMAGNET

A SOLENOID is a long coil of many circular turns of insulated wire wound closely. When current flows, the field inside a long solenoid is strong and UNIFORM, and the field-line pattern outside is just like that of a bar magnet - one end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole (found using the right-hand thumb rule applied to the turns). Inside the solenoid the lines are parallel, showing a uniform field.

If a piece of soft iron is placed inside the solenoid, the iron becomes strongly magnetised and the combination is called an ELECTROMAGNET. The magnetism lasts only while the current flows, so an electromagnet can be switched on and off. Its strength is increased by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, and using a soft-iron core. Soft iron is used (not steel) because it magnetises strongly but loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops, which is exactly what a temporary magnet needs. Electromagnets are used in electric bells, relays, cranes that lift scrap iron, loudspeakers and many machines.

17.7 FORCE ON A CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR IN A MAGNETIC FIELD

Since a current produces a magnetic field, a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field experiences a FORCE (this is the action-reaction partner of Oersted's effect). The force is largest when the conductor is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel to the field. The magnitude of the force increases with the current and with the strength of the field. The DIRECTION of the force is given by:
 - FLEMING'S LEFT-HAND RULE: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular. If the FOREfinger points along the FIELD and the MIddle finger along the (conventional) CURRENT, then the THumb points in the direction of the THrust (force/motion) on the conductor.

17.8 THE ELECTRIC MOTOR

An electric MOTOR converts electrical energy into mechanical (rotational) energy. PRINCIPLE: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a force (Fleming's left-hand rule) and therefore a turning effect (torque).
CONSTRUCTION: a rectangular coil ABCD of insulated wire is mounted on an axle between the poles of a permanent magnet. The two ends of the coil are connected to the two halves of a SPLIT-RING COMMUTATOR, which presses against carbon BRUSHES connected to the battery.
WORKING: current flows through the coil; the two sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions, so by Fleming's left-hand rule one side is pushed up and the other pushed down - the coil rotates. After each half turn the commutator reverses the current direction in the coil. This reversal keeps the force on each side in the right sense so that the coil continues to rotate in the same direction instead of stopping. Thus the split-ring commutator is the device that reverses the current after every half rotation.

17.9 ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION - FARADAY'S EXPERIMENTS

If a current produces magnetism, can magnetism produce a current? Michael Faraday answered yes in 1831. In his experiments a coil was connected to a sensitive galvanometer (no battery). When a bar magnet was pushed INTO the coil, the galvanometer needle deflected, showing a current; when the magnet was pulled OUT, the needle deflected the other way; when the magnet was held STILL inside the coil, there was NO current. A current was also induced when a second coil's current was switched on or off near the first coil.

The conclusion is the law of ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION: whenever the magnetic field (the number of field lines) linked with a coil CHANGES, an electric current is INDUCED in the coil. The induced current lasts only as long as the change continues. It is the RELATIVE MOTION (change) between the magnet and the coil that matters - a faster change gives a larger induced current.

FLEMING'S RIGHT-HAND RULE gives the direction of the induced current: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the RIGHT hand mutually perpendicular. If the FOREfinger points along the FIELD and the THumb along the direction of MOTION of the conductor, then the MIddle finger points along the direction of the induced CURRENT.

17.10 THE ELECTRIC GENERATOR

An electric GENERATOR (dynamo) converts mechanical energy into electrical energy - the reverse of the motor. PRINCIPLE: electromagnetic induction. A coil is rotated mechanically in a magnetic field; the changing field linkage induces a current in the coil (direction found by Fleming's right-hand rule).
AC GENERATOR: the coil ends are joined to two separate SLIP RINGS that press on brushes. As the coil rotates, the current in the external circuit reverses direction every half turn, producing ALTERNATING CURRENT (AC).
DC GENERATOR: the slip rings are replaced by a SPLIT-RING COMMUTATOR (as in the motor). The commutator reverses the connections every half turn so that the current in the external circuit always flows in the SAME direction, producing DIRECT CURRENT (DC).

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN AC AND DC: In alternating current (AC) the direction of flow reverses periodically (in India 50 times per second, i.e. 50 Hz); in direct current (DC) the flow is always in one direction. AC can be transmitted over long distances with little loss and its voltage can be stepped up or down with transformers, which is why mains electricity is AC. A cell or battery gives DC.

17.11 DOMESTIC ELECTRIC CIRCUITS

Electricity reaches a house through a pair of insulated wires. The main supply has three wires:
 - LIVE wire (usually red/brown insulation) - at high potential, carries the supply.
 - NEUTRAL wire (black/blue) - at nearly zero potential, completes the circuit.
 - EARTH wire (green/yellow) - connected to a metal plate buried in the ground; a safety wire.
The potential difference of the domestic supply in India is about 220 V. Inside the house the wires pass through a main fuse and an electricity meter, then to a distribution box. Appliances are connected in PARALLEL between live and neutral so that each gets the full 220 V and can be switched independently; the switch is always placed in the LIVE wire.

17.12 FUSE, OVERLOADING, SHORT-CIRCUITING

A FUSE is a short piece of thin wire of an alloy of low melting point, connected in SERIES in the live wire. If the current exceeds a safe value, the heat produced melts the fuse wire, breaking the circuit and protecting the wiring and appliances. The rating of a fuse is the maximum current it can carry without melting.
OVERLOADING happens when too many high-power appliances are run from one socket, so the total current exceeds the safe value - the wires heat up and may cause a fire. SHORT-CIRCUITING happens when the live and neutral wires touch directly (for example, when their insulation is damaged); the resistance becomes very small, so a very large current flows suddenly. In both cases the fuse melts (or the MCB trips) and cuts off the supply.
A MINIATURE CIRCUIT BREAKER (MCB) is a modern switch-like device used instead of a fuse. It automatically switches off (trips) when the current exceeds the safe value and can simply be reset by flipping it back on - it does not have to be replaced like a fuse.

17.13 EARTHING AND ELECTRICAL SAFETY

EARTHING (grounding) means connecting the metal body of an appliance to the earth through the earth wire. Normally the metal body carries no current. But if the live wire accidentally touches the metal body (a fault), the appliance body would become live and could give a fatal shock to anyone who touches it. The earth wire provides a low-resistance path for this fault current to flow safely into the ground; the large fault current also melts the fuse and disconnects the supply. Thus earthing protects the user from electric shock. Other safety practices: use correctly rated fuses, never overload sockets, use insulated tools, and switch off the mains before repairs.

SUMMARY

 - Oersted showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field; this links electricity and magnetism.
 - Magnetic field lines run from N to S outside a magnet, never cross, and are crowded where the field is strong.
 - The field around a straight wire is in concentric circles; its direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule (Maxwell's corkscrew rule).
 - A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet; with a soft-iron core it becomes an electromagnet whose magnetism can be switched on and off.
 - A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force; its direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule. This is the principle of the electric motor, which uses a split-ring commutator to keep the coil rotating one way.
 - Faraday's electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field linked with a coil induces a current; direction by Fleming's right-hand rule. This is the principle of the electric generator (AC with slip rings, DC with a commutator).
 - The domestic circuit uses live, neutral and earth wires; the fuse/MCB protects against overloading and short-circuiting, and earthing protects the user against shock.

chapter_summary.title: Magnetic Effect of Electric Current - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 17. It links electricity and magnetism: Oersted's discovery that current produces a magnetic field, the rules that give the field's direction (right-hand thumb rule, Fleming's rules), the electromagnet, the force on a current that drives the electric motor, Faraday's electromagnetic induction that drives the electric generator, and the wiring and safety of the domestic electric circuit.

sections.heading: Magnetic field and field lines
bullets: A magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel, unlike poles attract; poles always occur in pairs.
The magnetic field is the region around a magnet or current where its influence is felt; its direction is that in which a tiny compass north pole points.
Magnetic field lines run from N to S outside the magnet (S to N inside, forming closed loops), are crowded where the field is strong, and never cross one another.

sections.heading: Magnetic field due to electric current
bullets: Oersted's experiment: a current deflects a nearby compass needle, proving that current produces a magnetic field.
The field around a straight conductor is in concentric circles; its direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule (or Maxwell's corkscrew rule).
A circular loop has a field perpendicular to its plane at the centre; a solenoid behaves like a bar magnet, with a strong uniform field inside.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft-iron core; it is magnetic only while current flows and is stronger with more turns, more current and a soft-iron core.

sections.heading: Force on a conductor and the electric motor
bullets: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force; it is maximum when the conductor is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel.
Fleming's left-hand rule: forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = thrust (force).
An electric motor converts electrical energy into rotation; the force on the two sides of the coil makes it spin.
The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic induction and the generator
bullets: Faraday: when the magnetic field linked with a coil changes, a current is induced in it; the induced current lasts only while the change continues.
Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of the induced current: forefinger = field, thumb = motion, middle finger = induced current.
An electric generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field.
An AC generator uses slip rings (current reverses each half turn); a DC generator uses a split-ring commutator (current stays one-directional).

sections.heading: Domestic electric circuit and safety
bullets: The domestic supply uses three wires: live (high potential), neutral (near zero) and earth (safety); the supply is about 220 V AC.
Appliances are connected in parallel; the switch and the fuse are placed in the live wire.
A fuse (or MCB) melts/trips and breaks the circuit when the current is too high, protecting against overloading and short-circuiting.
Earthing connects an appliance's metal body to the ground, providing a safe path for fault current and protecting the user from electric shock.

key_takeaways: Oersted showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field, linking electricity and magnetism.
The field of a straight wire is in concentric circles; its direction follows the right-hand thumb rule, and a solenoid acts like a bar magnet.
An electromagnet (solenoid + soft-iron core) is magnetic only while current flows and can be switched on and off.
A current-carrying conductor in a field feels a force (Fleming's left-hand rule); this drives the electric motor, whose commutator reverses the current each half turn.
Faraday's electromagnetic induction (a changing field induces a current; Fleming's right-hand rule) is the principle of the electric generator.
An AC generator uses slip rings and a DC generator a split-ring commutator; AC reverses direction periodically while DC flows one way.
The domestic circuit's fuse/MCB guards against overloading and short-circuiting, and earthing protects the user from electric shock.

glossary.definition: The region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor in which a magnetic force can be detected; a vector quantity whose SI unit is the tesla (T).
Imaginary lines used to picture a magnetic field; they run from N to S outside a magnet, never cross, and are crowded where the field is strong.
The 1820 experiment showing that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle, proving that current produces a magnetic field.
Grasp a wire with the right hand, thumb along the current; the curled fingers point in the direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire.
A long coil of many closely wound circular turns of insulated wire; when carrying current it behaves like a bar magnet with a uniform field inside.
A solenoid wound on a soft-iron core; it is magnetic only while current flows, so it can be switched on and off.
For the force on a current in a field: forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = thrust (force/motion); uses the left hand.
A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical (rotational) energy using the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
A device with two half-rings that reverses the current in a motor (or generator) coil every half rotation, keeping a motor turning one way / giving a DC output.
The production of an induced current in a coil whenever the magnetic field linked with it changes; discovered by Faraday in 1831.
For an induced current: forefinger = field, thumb = motion of the conductor, middle finger = induced current; uses the right hand.
A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field (electromagnetic induction).
Current whose direction reverses periodically (50 Hz in India); used for mains supply because it transmits over long distances with little loss.
A short piece of low-melting-point alloy wire in the live wire that melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.
Connecting the metal body of an appliance to the ground through the earth wire, giving a safe path for fault current and protecting the user from shock.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Magnetic Effect of Electric Current (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) Worksheet for Lesson 17. Attempt all questions. Draw labelled diagrams where helpful and state the rule you use for each direction.

questions.question: State the properties of magnetic field lines.
questions.answer: (1) Outside a magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole; inside the magnet they run from S to N, so every line is a closed loop. (2) The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field there. (3) Lines are crowded together where the field is strong and spread out where it is weak. (4) Two field lines never cross each other - if they did, the field would have two directions at one point, which is impossible.
questions.explanation: Four standard properties of magnetic field lines.

questions.question: Describe Oersted's experiment and state what it proved.
questions.answer: Oersted placed a compass needle below a straight wire aligned north-south. With no current the needle stayed parallel to the wire. When a current was switched on, the needle was deflected; reversing the current reversed the deflection. This proved that an electric current produces a magnetic field around itself - linking electricity and magnetism.
questions.explanation: Setup, observation on switching/reversing current, and the conclusion.

questions.question: State the right-hand thumb rule and use it to describe the field around a straight current-carrying wire.
questions.answer: Right-hand thumb rule: grasp the wire with the right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of the conventional current; the curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines. Around a long straight wire the field lines are concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire, stronger (more crowded) near the wire and weaker farther away.
questions.explanation: State the rule, then apply it to the concentric-circle pattern.

questions.question: What is an electromagnet? List three factors that increase its strength and state why soft iron is used for the core.
questions.answer: An electromagnet is a solenoid wound on a soft-iron core; it is magnetic only while current flows. Its strength increases with (1) a larger current, (2) a greater number of turns, and (3) the use of a soft-iron core. Soft iron is used because it magnetises strongly when current flows but loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops, which is exactly what a temporary, switchable magnet needs (steel would retain magnetism).
questions.explanation: Definition, three factors, and the soft-iron reasoning.

questions.question: State Fleming's left-hand rule. A wire carries current from west to east in a magnetic field directed from south to north (horizontal). In which direction is the force?
questions.answer: Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = thrust (force). Here field points south-to-north and current points west-to-east; applying the rule, the force on the wire is directed vertically upward.
questions.explanation: State the rule, then apply it to the given directions.

questions.question: Explain the principle, construction and working of an electric motor. What is the function of the split-ring commutator?
questions.answer: Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a force (Fleming's left-hand rule) and hence a turning effect (torque). Construction: a rectangular coil of insulated wire is mounted on an axle between the poles of a permanent magnet; the coil ends are joined to the two halves of a split-ring commutator that presses on carbon brushes connected to a battery. Working: current flows through the coil; its two sides carry current in opposite directions, so one side is pushed up and the other down, and the coil rotates. After each half turn the commutator reverses the current in the coil so the force on each side stays in the right sense and the coil keeps turning in the same direction. Function of the split-ring commutator: it reverses the direction of current in the coil after every half rotation, which keeps the coil rotating continuously in one direction.
questions.explanation: Principle (force/torque), construction (coil, magnet, commutator, brushes), working, and the commutator's role.

questions.question: State the law of electromagnetic induction. In Faraday's experiment, why is there no current when the magnet is held stationary inside the coil?
questions.answer: Law of electromagnetic induction: whenever the magnetic field (number of field lines) linked with a coil changes, a current is induced in the coil, lasting only while the change continues. When the magnet is held stationary inside the coil, the field linked with the coil is not changing, so there is no induced current - it is the relative motion (change) between magnet and coil that produces the current.
questions.explanation: State the law; no change in flux means no induced current.

questions.question: Distinguish between an AC generator and a DC generator. State two differences between alternating and direct current.
questions.answer: Both generators convert mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field (electromagnetic induction). The difference is in how the coil connects to the external circuit: an AC generator uses two separate slip rings, so the current in the external circuit reverses every half turn (alternating current); a DC generator uses a split-ring commutator, which reverses the connections every half turn so that the external current always flows in one direction (direct current). Differences between AC and DC: (1) AC reverses its direction periodically (50 Hz in India) while DC flows always in one direction. (2) AC voltage can be stepped up or down by transformers and transmitted over long distances with little loss, whereas DC (from a cell) cannot be easily transformed.
questions.explanation: Slip rings vs split-ring commutator; two AC/DC differences.

questions.question: Name the three wires in a domestic circuit and state the function of the earth wire.
questions.answer: The three wires are the live wire (high potential, carries the supply), the neutral wire (near zero potential, completes the circuit) and the earth wire (connected to a metal plate in the ground). The earth wire is a safety wire: it connects the metal body of an appliance to the ground, so if the live wire accidentally touches the body, the fault current flows safely to earth (and melts the fuse) instead of giving the user an electric shock.
questions.explanation: Live/neutral/earth identification plus the safety function of earthing.

questions.question: Distinguish between overloading and short-circuiting, and state how a fuse protects the circuit.
questions.answer: Overloading occurs when too many high-power appliances draw current from one socket so the total current exceeds the safe value, heating the wires. Short-circuiting occurs when the live and neutral wires touch directly (e.g. damaged insulation), making the resistance very small so a sudden very large current flows. A fuse is a thin low-melting-point wire connected in series in the live wire; when the current exceeds the safe value, the heat melts the fuse wire and breaks the circuit, cutting off the supply and protecting the wiring and appliances.
questions.explanation: Define both faults, then the fuse's protective action.

questions.question: What is a magnetic field?
questions.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor in which its magnetic influence (force) can be detected. It is a vector quantity; its direction at a point is the direction in which the north pole of a small test compass would point, and its SI unit is the tesla.
questions.explanation: Region of influence; direction via compass north pole.

questions.question: Why can two magnetic field lines never intersect?
questions.answer: If two field lines crossed at a point, then at that point the magnetic field would have two different directions (one along each line). A field can have only one direction at a given point, so this is impossible. Hence field lines never intersect.
questions.explanation: One field direction per point.

questions.question: State two properties of magnetic field lines.
questions.answer: (1) They run from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet (S to N inside), forming closed loops. (2) They are crowded where the field is strong and spread out where it is weak. (They also never cross, and the tangent gives the field direction.)
questions.explanation: Any two valid properties.

questions.question: What did Oersted's experiment demonstrate?
questions.answer: It demonstrated that an electric current produces a magnetic field. When current flowed through a wire, a nearby compass needle was deflected; reversing the current reversed the deflection. This established the link between electricity and magnetism.
questions.explanation: Current produces magnetism.

questions.question: State the right-hand thumb rule.
questions.answer: Grasp the current-carrying wire with the right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of the conventional current. The curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines circling the wire.
questions.explanation: Thumb = current, fingers = field.

questions.question: Describe the magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying conductor.
questions.answer: They are concentric circles lying in planes perpendicular to the wire and centred on it. The circles are crowded (field strong) close to the wire and spread out (field weak) farther away. The field also increases if the current increases.
questions.explanation: Concentric circles; stronger near the wire.

questions.question: How does the magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil depend on the number of turns and the current?
questions.answer: The field at the centre increases when the number of turns is increased (each turn adds its own field) and when the current is increased. It also increases if the radius of the loop is made smaller.
questions.explanation: More turns, more current, smaller radius -> stronger field.

questions.question: Why does a current-carrying solenoid behave like a bar magnet?
questions.answer: In a solenoid the fields of all the turns add up, giving a strong uniform field inside and a pattern of field lines outside that is exactly like a bar magnet's - one end behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole. So a current-carrying solenoid acts as a bar magnet.
questions.explanation: Fields of turns add; ends act as N and S poles.

questions.question: How would you find which end of a current-carrying solenoid is the north pole?
questions.answer: Apply the right-hand thumb rule (clock rule) to the turns: look at one end of the solenoid; if the current flows anticlockwise as you look at that end, it is the north pole, and if it flows clockwise, that end is the south pole. Equivalently, curl the right-hand fingers along the current direction and the thumb points to the N pole.
questions.explanation: Anticlockwise current as seen = N pole.

questions.question: What is an electromagnet?
questions.answer: An electromagnet is a solenoid wound on a soft-iron core. When current flows through the coil, the iron becomes strongly magnetised; the magnetism lasts only while the current flows, so the electromagnet can be switched on and off.
questions.explanation: Solenoid + soft-iron core; temporary magnet.

questions.question: List the factors that determine the strength of an electromagnet.
questions.answer: Its strength increases with (1) a larger current through the coil, (2) a greater number of turns in the coil, and (3) the use of a soft-iron core (rather than air or steel).
questions.explanation: Current, number of turns, soft-iron core.

questions.question: Why is soft iron, and not steel, used for the core of an electromagnet?
questions.answer: Soft iron magnetises strongly when current flows but loses almost all of its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off. This is exactly what is needed for a temporary, switchable magnet. Steel retains its magnetism after the current stops, so it cannot be switched off and would behave as a permanent magnet.
questions.explanation: Soft iron is a temporary magnet; steel is permanent.

questions.question: Give two practical uses of electromagnets.
questions.answer: (1) In cranes used to lift heavy iron and steel scrap (switched off to release the load). (2) In electric bells, relays and loudspeakers. (Any valid uses such as in MRI machines or magnetic separators are acceptable.)
questions.explanation: Two valid applications.

questions.question: State Fleming's left-hand rule.
questions.answer: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the middle finger along the conventional current, then the thumb points in the direction of the force (thrust) on the conductor.
questions.explanation: Forefinger field, middle current, thumb thrust.

questions.question: On what factors does the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field depend, and when is it maximum?
questions.answer: The force increases with the current through the conductor and with the strength of the magnetic field. It is maximum when the conductor is perpendicular to the field and zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.
questions.explanation: Current, field strength, angle; max at 90 degrees.

questions.question: A conductor carries current vertically upward in a horizontal magnetic field pointing north. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force.
questions.answer: Point the forefinger north (field) and the middle finger upward (current); the thumb then points to the west. So the force on the conductor is directed towards the west.
questions.explanation: Apply the left-hand rule to the given directions.

questions.question: What happens to the force on a current-carrying conductor if (a) the current is reversed, (b) both the current and the field are reversed?
questions.answer: (a) Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force. (b) Reversing both the current and the field reverses the force twice, so the two reversals cancel and the force is in the same direction as before.
questions.explanation: Single reversal flips force; double reversal restores it.

questions.question: What energy conversion takes place in an electric motor?
questions.answer: An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical (rotational) energy.
questions.explanation: Electrical to mechanical.

questions.question: State the principle of an electric motor.
questions.answer: The principle is that a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a force (Fleming's left-hand rule), which produces a turning effect (torque) that rotates the coil.
questions.explanation: Force/torque on a current loop in a field.

questions.question: What is the function of the split-ring commutator in an electric motor?
questions.answer: The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current through the coil after every half rotation. This keeps the force on each side of the coil in the correct sense so that the coil continues to rotate in the same direction instead of stopping or reversing.
questions.explanation: Reverses current each half turn to maintain rotation.

questions.question: Why do the two sides of a motor coil experience forces in opposite directions?
questions.answer: In the two sides of the coil the current flows in opposite directions, while both lie in the same magnetic field. By Fleming's left-hand rule, opposite current directions in the same field give forces in opposite directions - one side is pushed up and the other down, producing a turning effect.
questions.explanation: Opposite currents in same field -> opposite forces.

questions.question: Without a commutator, what would happen to the rotating coil of a motor?
questions.answer: Without the commutator the current direction in the coil would stay fixed. After the coil turns half a revolution, the forces would act to push it back, so the coil would only oscillate or come to rest at the half-turn position instead of rotating continuously. The commutator reverses the current each half turn to keep it spinning in one direction.
questions.explanation: No reversal -> coil stalls/oscillates.

questions.question: State the law of electromagnetic induction.
questions.answer: Whenever the magnetic field (number of field lines) linked with a coil changes, an electric current is induced in the coil. The induced current lasts only as long as the change continues.
questions.explanation: Changing flux induces a current.

questions.question: Describe one of Faraday's experiments demonstrating electromagnetic induction.
questions.answer: A coil is connected to a sensitive galvanometer (no battery). When a bar magnet is pushed into the coil, the galvanometer deflects, showing an induced current; when the magnet is pulled out, it deflects the other way; when the magnet is held still inside, there is no deflection. This shows that a changing magnetic field induces a current.
questions.explanation: Magnet moved relative to a coil induces current.

questions.question: State Fleming's right-hand rule.
questions.answer: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the thumb along the direction of motion of the conductor, then the middle finger points in the direction of the induced current.
questions.explanation: Forefinger field, thumb motion, middle induced current.

questions.question: Why is there no induced current when a magnet is held stationary inside a coil?
questions.answer: An induced current requires the magnetic field linked with the coil to change. When the magnet is stationary inside the coil, the field linkage is constant - it is not changing - so no current is induced. Current appears only when the magnet (or field) moves relative to the coil.
questions.explanation: No change in flux means no induced current.

questions.question: What is the function of an electric generator?
questions.answer: An electric generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. A coil is rotated mechanically in a magnetic field, and electromagnetic induction produces an electric current in the coil.
questions.explanation: Mechanical to electrical via induction.

questions.question: How does a DC generator differ from an AC generator in construction?
questions.answer: An AC generator connects the coil to the external circuit through two separate slip rings, so the output current reverses every half turn (alternating current). A DC generator instead uses a split-ring commutator, which reverses the connections every half turn so the output current always flows in one direction (direct current).
questions.explanation: Slip rings (AC) vs split-ring commutator (DC).

questions.question: State two differences between alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC).
questions.answer: (1) AC reverses its direction periodically (50 times per second in India), whereas DC flows always in one direction. (2) AC voltage can be stepped up or down by a transformer and transmitted over long distances with little loss, whereas DC cannot be easily transformed; a cell/battery gives DC.
questions.explanation: Direction reversal and transformability.

questions.question: Explain how earthing protects a user from electric shock.
questions.answer: The earth wire connects the metal body of an appliance to a metal plate buried in the ground. If the live wire accidentally touches the metal body, the fault current flows through the low-resistance earth wire safely into the ground (and the large current melts the fuse, cutting off the supply) instead of passing through a person who touches the appliance. Thus the user is protected from a fatal shock.
questions.explanation: Earth wire diverts fault current to the ground.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. In 1820 Oersted noticed that a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire was deflected. Later studies showed that the field around a straight wire forms concentric circles, while a coil of many turns wound closely (a solenoid) produces a field like that of a bar magnet. (a) What did Oersted's observation prove? (b) What is the shape of the field lines around a straight wire? (c) Name the rule used to find the field direction around a straight wire. (d) How does a current-carrying solenoid behave?
questions.answer: (a) It proved that an electric current produces a magnetic field around itself, linking electricity and magnetism. (b) The field lines are concentric circles, in planes perpendicular to the wire and centred on it. (c) The right-hand thumb rule (or Maxwell's corkscrew rule). (d) A current-carrying solenoid behaves like a bar magnet, with one end a north pole and the other a south pole and a strong uniform field inside.
questions.explanation: Covers Oersted, field shape, the rule, and the solenoid.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. A scrap-yard crane lifts heavy pieces of iron and releases them on demand. It uses a coil wound on a soft-iron core that is energised by current. (a) What is this device called? (b) Why is a soft-iron core used instead of steel? (c) State two ways to make it lift heavier loads. (d) Why is such a magnet preferred to a permanent magnet for this job?
questions.answer: (a) It is an electromagnet. (b) Soft iron magnetises strongly when current flows but loses its magnetism when the current stops, so the load can be released; steel would stay magnetised. (c) Increase the current and increase the number of turns in the coil (a soft-iron core also helps). (d) Its magnetism can be switched on and off and its strength varied, so the crane can pick up and then drop the scrap on demand - a permanent magnet could not release it.
questions.explanation: Electromagnet identification, soft-iron reasoning, strength factors, on/off advantage.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. A straight horizontal wire carries a current and is placed between the poles of a horseshoe magnet so that the field points from the north pole to the south pole. When the current is switched on, the wire jumps. (a) Name the effect responsible. (b) Which rule gives the direction of the force? (c) If the current is reversed, what happens to the direction of the jump? (d) When is this force zero?
questions.answer: (a) The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (the motor effect). (b) Fleming's left-hand rule (forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force). (c) Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force, so the wire jumps the opposite way. (d) The force is zero when the wire is placed parallel to the magnetic field.
questions.explanation: Motor effect, left-hand rule, reversal, zero-force condition.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. An electric motor has a rectangular coil placed between the poles of a magnet. The coil is connected through a split-ring commutator and brushes to a battery, and the coil rotates steadily. (a) What energy conversion does the motor perform? (b) State the principle of the motor. (c) What is the role of the split-ring commutator? (d) Why do the two sides of the coil move in opposite directions?
questions.answer: (a) It converts electrical energy into mechanical (rotational) energy. (b) A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a force (Fleming's left-hand rule) that produces a turning effect. (c) The commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn so that the coil keeps rotating in the same direction. (d) The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, so by Fleming's left-hand rule the forces on them are opposite - one side is pushed up and the other down, giving a turning effect.
questions.explanation: Energy conversion, principle, commutator, opposite forces.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. A coil is joined to a galvanometer with no battery. A student moves a bar magnet towards the coil, then holds it still inside, then pulls it away. (a) What is observed when the magnet moves towards the coil? (b) What is observed when the magnet is held still? (c) Name the phenomenon involved. (d) Which rule gives the direction of the induced current?
questions.answer: (a) The galvanometer needle deflects, showing an induced current flows while the magnet approaches. (b) When the magnet is held still inside the coil there is no deflection - no current is induced because the field linkage is not changing. (c) Electromagnetic induction (Faraday). (d) Fleming's right-hand rule (forefinger = field, thumb = motion, middle finger = induced current).
questions.explanation: Induction experiment outcomes, the phenomenon, and the rule.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. A generator rotates a coil in a magnetic field to supply electricity. One version connects the coil through two slip rings; another connects it through a split-ring commutator. (a) What energy conversion takes place in a generator? (b) Which version produces alternating current? (c) Which version produces direct current? (d) State one reason why mains supply is AC.
questions.answer: (a) A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. (b) The version with two slip rings produces alternating current (AC). (c) The version with a split-ring commutator produces direct current (DC). (d) AC can be stepped up or down by transformers and transmitted over long distances with very little energy loss, which is why the mains supply is AC.
questions.explanation: Energy conversion, slip rings vs commutator, why AC mains.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. A house is wired with three wires - live, neutral and earth. A fuse is fitted, and all appliances' metal bodies are connected to the earth wire. (a) Which wire is at high potential? (b) Where is the fuse connected and what does it do? (c) What is the purpose of the earth wire? (d) What is short-circuiting?
questions.answer: (a) The live wire is at high potential. (b) The fuse is connected in series in the live wire; it melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value, protecting the wiring and appliances. (c) The earth wire connects an appliance's metal body to the ground, giving a safe path for fault current and protecting the user from electric shock. (d) Short-circuiting is when the live and neutral wires touch directly, so the resistance becomes very small and a sudden very large current flows.
questions.explanation: Live wire, fuse, earthing, short-circuit definition.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. In a kitchen, several high-power appliances are plugged into one socket. After some time the fuse melts. (a) What is this situation called? (b) Why did the fuse melt? (c) How is this different from a short circuit? (d) Name a modern device that can be used instead of a fuse and reset after tripping.
questions.answer: (a) This is overloading - drawing more current than the circuit is rated for. (b) The total current of all the appliances exceeded the safe value, so the heat produced melted the low-melting-point fuse wire, breaking the circuit. (c) In a short circuit the live and neutral wires touch directly, giving a very small resistance and a sudden huge current; overloading is a gradual build-up of current from too many appliances. (d) A miniature circuit breaker (MCB), which trips automatically and can be reset by flipping it back on.
questions.explanation: Overloading vs short circuit; the MCB.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. Iron filings sprinkled on a card over a bar magnet arrange themselves into curved patterns running between the poles. (a) What do these patterns represent? (b) From which pole to which pole do they run outside the magnet? (c) Where are the lines most crowded? (d) Can two of these lines cross?
questions.answer: (a) They represent the magnetic field lines (lines of force) of the magnet. (b) Outside the magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole (and from S to N inside). (c) They are most crowded near the poles, where the field is strongest. (d) No - two field lines can never cross, because the field can have only one direction at any point.
questions.explanation: Field-line representation, direction, crowding, no crossing.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. A vertical wire passes up through a horizontal card; current flows upward. Iron filings on the card form circles around the wire, and a compass placed on the card points along a circle. (a) What is the shape of the field around the wire? (b) Using the right-hand thumb rule with current upward, in which sense (clockwise/anticlockwise, viewed from above) do the field lines point? (c) What happens to the compass if the current is reversed? (d) How does the field change closer to the wire?
questions.answer: (a) The field lines are concentric circles around the wire, in the plane of the card. (b) With the right thumb pointing up (current), the curled fingers point anticlockwise when viewed from above, so the field lines are anticlockwise. (c) Reversing the current reverses the field direction, so the compass needle turns to point the opposite way (clockwise sense). (d) The field is stronger closer to the wire (the circles are more crowded) and weaker farther away.
questions.explanation: Field shape, right-hand rule sense, reversal, distance dependence.
